chapter: Brass bands, union and theatre work
title: Brass band work and the union
summary: Barnes says he played most brass bands but fell away after quarrelling over union dues.

people.name: Lawrence (trumpet player in Barnes's small-club bands)

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: You know something we haven't hit is those brass bands that you played with. How many brass bands have you played with through the years? I played with most of the brass bands.
Just lately here I started playing a couple years ago.
Well I know you played some for Andrew Jefferson since I've been down here.
Did you ever play E flat there in that?
I had E flat, I know what would come with it. I had E flat, I had E flat concert, what Parker gave me. What did Parker gave you? Gave me. E flat concert, let me tell you that right now.
Did you ever play in any of those famous bands like Tuxedo?

Oh yeah, there's the Harlot band I ever played in here. I played most every band on here. Yeah, I'm not no complainant on the band. Lately here since I've got, I'm about, about two or three years, maybe three years I've leave now. Then what kept me more from the band is this. I went down the union. I went down the union. I jumped the union but I wouldn't pay no dues no. I went down the jackpot, eh. I wasn't a talking up to who you ought to do this stuff. I found the union. I had my own band going the same thing. Well you all give me no work. Yeah.
Well how about when you and Lawrence were playing together, were you in the union then? Well, these little jobs all around town? No.
No. Well, the union's a late thing anyway, Marlowe, for speaking to you. Well, the union's alright.
I don't want to talk about the tennis or not. But, uh, the main town in the fair. Yeah.
